extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, judges, and law students studying evidence and defenses in U.S. patent infringement litigation
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and evidentiary rules governing common defenses to patent infringement suits (inventorship, reissue, specification sufficiency, claim scope, title, surrender/repeal, and noninfringement), as explained in a legal treatise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recitals of oath in patent prima facie evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: In the absence of fraud the patent recitals are conclusive evidence that proper oaths were taken.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discovery among the papers of an unfilled blank form of oath does not overcome the prima facie proof arising from the recital that the oath was taken (cases cited: Seymour v. Osborne; Crompton v. Belknap Mills).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent grant void when it exceeds Patent Office jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Grants that exceed the jurisdiction of the Patent Office (for example, issuing letters-patent to a sole patentee for a joint invention or vice versa, or allowing reissues that include new inventions) are void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prima facie the patent is correct and valid; defendant can overcome it only by the clearest and most reliable testimony. A comparison of the challenged grant with proper standards (and relevant case law) is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint vs sole patent validity (inventorship disputes)
rubrics_metrics.description: A joint patent for a sole invention is void; a sole patent for a joint invention is also void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The patent is prima facie correct; the burden of proof rests on the defendant to show by clear and convincing evidence that the patentee was not the sole inventor or was a joint inventor. Prior foreign patents inconsistent with the domestic patent do not change this burden—the American patent generally prevails absent conclusive extraneous evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumptions from joint applications and assignments
rubrics_metrics.description: A joint application raises a presumption that the applicants are joint inventors; an assignment or the patent itself raises prima facie evidence of title or inventorship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These presumptions can be rebutted by proof. Defenses alleging lack of joint inventorship are disfavored unless patentees acted disingenuously or misled the defendant (authorities cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence to prove joint or sole inventive act
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventive act is joint when conception evolved by mutual consultations, suggestions, experiments; sole when conception arose in one mind even if aided by others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence of sole inventorship: contemporaneous descriptions, drawings, models, testimony detailing steps. Evidence of joint inventorship: absence of any memorandum of a complete idea before consultation, joint efforts and successes. The law tends to recognize joint merits where any unity of endeavor existed; once a patent issues, the presumption of correctness is strong and can be counteracted only by conclusive proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose and limits of reissue
rubrics_metrics.description: The jurisdiction to allow reissues exists solely to enable an inventor to correct a defective patent, not to extend an existing patent to new inventions or to cover inventions intentionally omitted from the original patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims of the reissue must be confined to inventions not advertently excluded from the original claims. A reissue that covers new matter must be cured by disclaimer or fails; if reissue claims matter disclosed but not claimed originally, the question of intentional exclusion and reasonable delay in seeking amendment arises.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to show a reissue departs from the original
rubrics_metrics.description: Departure of the reissue from the original is shown by comparing the two patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defendant should introduce the original patent and may use expert evidence, file copies, and Patent Office models to point out differences. If the reissue includes new matter, disclaimer may cure it; if matter was intentionally excluded earlier, further evidence about the inventor's knowledge and delay is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of delay in seeking reissue/amendment
rubrics_metrics.description: A delay in seeking reissue or amendment may be fatal unless plaintiff proves original inadvertence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether a delay is reasonable is a legal question for the court based on the facts; unavoidable delay is not unreasonable. Plaintiff must show when he discovered the error and why he postponed amendment; defendant may prove an earlier discovery date or that the delay was unjustified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weight of Patent Office decision on reissue identity
rubrics_metrics.description: The decision of the Commissioner allowing the reissue is of great weight with the court and the re-issued patent is prima facie evidence that the reissue is legal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nevertheless, courts will depart from the Commissioner's decision upon clear proof; evidence of what passed in the Patent Office pending the original application is admissible on identity questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical objections to patents strictly construed
rubrics_metrics.description: Technical objections to patents are to be strictly construed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts will not lightly invalidate patents on technicalities; substantive proof is required to overcome the presumptions favoring the patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tenth defence: claimed invention not statutory subject matter
rubrics_metrics.description: The defence that the patented invention is not embraced in any one of the statutory classes protected by Acts of Congress challenges patentable subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The patent raises a presumption that the claimed invention is patentable subject matter; the defendant must rebut this. These are principally legal questions of patent construction and class definitions, and the court may decide them without a jury.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eleventh defence: fraudulent specification (concealment/redundancy and intent)
rubrics_metrics.description: Allegation that the specification contains less than the whole truth (concealment) or more than necessary (redundancy) with intent to deceive the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two elements must be proven: (1) concealment or redundancy (established by expert or practical mechanic testimony showing a skilled person could not practice the invention from the disclosure, or that following the specification imposes unnecessary expense or less effective steps); and (2) intent to deceive (inferred from circumstances such as knowledge of better methods, secret instructions to licensees, contemporaneous declarations). Both elements must be clearly proved to a jury; patent is prima facie evidence for plaintiff and burden rests on defendant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards of proof for intent to deceive
rubrics_metrics.description: Intent to deceive in connection with a fraudulent specification is generally inferred from circumstances rather than proved directly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If facts concealed are so important that the inventor must have known a mechanic could not construct the invention from the description, or if the inventor used secret better methods, intent may be fairly presumed. Contemporaneous declarations or secret instructions are admissible. The jury must be satisfied of intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Twelfth defence: ambiguity of description (enablement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Allegation that the disclosure is ambiguous and does not enable persons skilled in the art to practice the invention without exercising inventive faculties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent is prima facie sufficient; defendant must provide satisfactory evidence—testimony of practical mechanics who attempted to construct and use the invention by following the patent is most persuasive. Scientific experts are proper too. No inquiry into inventor's intent arises under this defence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence weight: practical mechanic vs scientific expert
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence of a practical mechanic's single success or failure in using the specification is of greater weight than numerous contrary opinions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A single real-world attempt that succeeds or fails is more convincing on enablement/ambiguity issues than multiple hypothetical or purely academic opinions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thirteenth defence: excessive claims and cure by disclaimer
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim asserted to be excessive (covers more than the actual invention) and not cured by disclaimer within a reasonable time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court construes claims as a matter of law and instructs the jury on the nature of the invention; the jury determines if the claim includes more than the actual invention. Patent is prima facie evidence of correctness of the claim; defendant must prove the essential characteristics of the true invention showing the claim covers more. If disclaimer is filed promptly upon discovery the excess may be cured; plaintiff bears burden to show disclaimer filed without unreasonable delay or that reasonable time has not elapsed since discovery. An inventor is not chargeable with notice of excess until judicial interpretation, unless excess is evident on its face.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonableness of delay in filing disclaimers
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether delay in filing a disclaimer or amendment is reasonable is a legal question for the court to decide on the facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unavoidable delay is not unreasonable; unavoidable but protracted delay may still be acceptable if public not misled and other interests not affected. Defendant may produce evidence fixing an earlier discovery date or showing unjustifiable delay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fourteenth defence: ambiguity of claim (claim construction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim is ambiguous when the court cannot ascertain from it what the patentee intended to protect; ambiguity is a question of law for the court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allowance by the Patent Office is prima facie that claims are not ambiguous, but courts will construe them and may consider extrinsic evidence (experts, persons in the art, Patent Office papers) at judicial discretion to render technical phraseology intelligible. When a claim depends on facts, the jury may be required to find those facts and then apply the court's construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fifteenth defence: surrender of the patent
rubrics_metrics.description: Allegation that the letters-patent have been surrendered to the government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Production of the patent by plaintiff is prima facie evidence it remains in force; the defendant must prove surrender by certified copies from Patent Office records showing surrender, ownership by the surrendering parties, cancellation, or replacement by re-issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sixteenth defence: repeal or annulment of the patent
rubrics_metrics.description: Allegation that the patent has been repealed or annulled in whole or part by a judgment or proceeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent is prima facie evidence for plaintiff; defendant may show repeal by authenticated copy of the judgment or by certified Patent Office record of cancellation, and may show the scope of any avoidance judgment by court records.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seventeenth defence: want of title in the plaintiff
rubrics_metrics.description: Denial of the plaintiff's legal title to the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When plaintiff is patentee, patent is prima facie evidence of ownership; where plaintiff is an assignee, burden rests on plaintiff to establish conveyances (original assignment admissible even if unrecorded). Certified copies from Patent Office are prima facie evidence of record contents. Defendant may attack the existence/validity of the conveyances or assert superior title acquired later without notice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eighteenth defence: nonidentity of infringing article (noninfringement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Denial that the defendant's product or process is identical with or included in the patented invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent is not prima facie evidence of infringement; the plaintiff must prove infringement by extraneous evidence. If the evidence on identity/infringement is equally balanced, the defendant prevails. Evidence typically includes specimens, drawings, descriptions, and expert testimony comparing accused device/process to the claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: General rule on burdens and presumptions in infringement litigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Throughout these defences the patent as issued furnishes prima facie evidence for the plaintiff on many points (validity, sufficiency of specification, non-ambiguity), but does not constitute prima facie evidence of infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whoever asserts a defense that contradicts a patent's prima facie position generally bears the burden of proof to rebut it; conversely, the plaintiff bears the burden of proving infringement by extraneous evidence.
